podcasts.title: European Defense Sovereignty Starts in the Factory: Stark’s Uwe Horstmann and Johannes Schaback
podcasts.description: Two years after its founding, Stark has roughly 700 employees and strike drones in the field in Ukraine. CEO Uwe Horstmann and CTO Johannes Schaback argue that the real lesson of that war is not any single weapon: the innovation ecosystem behind it is the wonder weapon. They explain why Stark designs every system for mass manufacturing from day one, runs 10 to 15 programs like a venture portfolio, and views the staff sergeant who operates a system as just as important as the general who buys it. Johannes recounts the publicly reported failed trial that became a forging moment, as engineers worked around the clock at a freezing test range until they landed three consecutive hits. They discuss NATO’s principles of responsible AI use and the hard-coded constraints in Stark’s autonomy stack. And Uwe lays out his next big idea: defense contracts structured like cloud contracts with surge capacity built in, so production itself becomes deterrence. Hosted by Pat Grady and Luciana Lixandru, Sequoia Capital Chapters 0:00 – Introduction 1:03 – Billions in contracts in 18 months: Stark's four-part playbook 2:28 – The staff sergeant matters as much as the general, and wood beats plastic 7:42 – Why Europe is ready for a neo prime, and why procurement reform will last 11:45 – Startup DNA, venture-style programs, and "as complex as a washing machine" 16:27 – Born out of fire: the failed trial and the round-the-clock comeback 21:13 – Where Stark finds talent, and why defense is no longer off-limits 23:48 – Anatomy of a strike, from the wooden crate to the kill zone 27:22 – Vertical integration, multiple domains, and shifting left on manufacturing 32:53 – After the Hugging Face hack: guardrails on autonomous weapons 35:56 – Matching the primes on R&D and scaling to 700 people in two years 39:24 – Deterrence by contract, and Europe's next chapter with the US

podcasts.name: No Priors
podcasts.title: Taking on ServiceNow: Coding Agents the Rest of Us with Serval Co-Founder and CEO Jake Stauch
podcasts.description: What happens when you put code-generation agents in the hands of enterprise IT teams? With Serval, you get a system where it's easy for everyone to be a builder. Sarah Guo and Elad Gil sit down with Serval co-founder and CEO Jake Stauch to analyze his company’s direct challenge to ServiceNow as the enterprise automation and service management system of record. Jake explains that by building an AI platform for enterprise IT departments with Serval, users can safely build while still safeguarding permissions by strict deterministic approvals and an audit trail. He also talks about ProServal, the company’s team that embeds automation engineers directly with customers in order to provide ongoing support and service. Jake also discusses how AI was the big unlock to taking on ServiceNow, why he’s betting on coding agents getting even better, why consumer is a window into what will happen next in enterprise and why the SaaS-pocalypse might look more like a consolidation, why background agents are still a moonshot in enterprise software, and the importance of hiring product-oriented engineers. podcasts.name: The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck
podcasts.title: State of AI 2026: The Biggest Stories of the Year (and AGI in 2027?) | Nathan Benaich
podcasts.description: AGI in 2027. That’s the last line of this year’s State of AI Report, and its author Nathan Benaich (Air Street Capital) is back for the third year to defend it. AI is now building AI: Claude leads 26% of Anthropic’s own model R&D, up from under 1% in February, but Nathan thinks “research taste” is the wall. OpenAI’s evaluation agents ended up inside Hugging Face’s systems, only a Chinese open-weight model could help investigate, and Nathan now argues cyber risk matters more than existential risk. Catching up to OpenAI or Anthropic from scratch costs about a trillion dollars, which is why “you either die trying to get to the frontier, or live long enough to serve inference.” Americans would rather live next to a nuclear plant than a data center, $50B of projects are stalled, and all 27 EU countries together have fewer GPUs than one top US cluster. Sovereign AI is “like a national airline: it’s still someone else’s airplane.” Also: the three-lab race and the fate of the neo labs, models vs. harnesses, why he won’t give a personal AI agent his credit card, the Codex adoption gap and why OpenAI should open a store, enterprises owning their own AI instead of renting it, and the morning a solo GP woke up to twelve expert interviews his agent ran overnight. podcasts.description: Subscribe to Every (free for 14 days): https://every.to/youtube-every-offer Can AI create good art? Fred Graver thinks the answer depends on you. The Emmy Award–winning writer, producer, and founder of AI Writer’s Studio says AI can help with many parts of the creative process—but it can’t give you something to say. Without your own point of view, AI will only make your work more average. On this week’s episode of The Every Podcast, Natalia Quintero sits down with Graver. They discuss why every writer should have a ‘who I am as a writer’ document, the cast of AI collaborators he’s built into his own writers’ room, and the human quirks that make characters endearing—the part he insists AI can’t supply. podcasts.title: Freedom of Action: America's ASI Strategy, w/ RAND's Joel Predd, Ben Boudreaux & Matt Chessen
podcasts.description: Joel Predd, Ben Boudreaux, and Matt Chessen of RAND's Center for the Geopolitics of AGI join Nathan to discuss their framework for maintaining freedom of action on the path to superintelligence. Analyzing seven strategic archetypes—including dominance, deterrence, co-development, and moratoriums—they argue that deep technological and geopolitical uncertainty makes defaulting to any single strategy dangerous. To avoid foreclosing critical options, their proposed approach calls for investing in long-lead capabilities like model verification, containment, agency evaluations, and an adaptable security architecture. At stake are decisive economic and military advantage, stable competition with rivals like China, and humanity's survival with agency.
